content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims at  link prediction over knowledge graphs. The idea is to first retrieve a relevant subgraph from the head entity and then do reasoning over this subgraph to find the answers with a core architecture of graph transformer. The authors perform experiments on standard link prediction benchmarks including WN18 and FB15k. The methods perform better or comparable with the methods they compare.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written and easy to follow. The figures are really illustrative for readers to comprehend. I like the tables that analyze the efficiency of different models.

The method seems to be overclaiming the task as the method is only doing link prediction over knowledge graphs. However, the paper tells a story about knowledge graph reasoning which traditionally refers to mining logical rules over knowledge graphs or answering complex logical queries over the graphs. I think the paper should be crystal clear in the title that the task is link prediction unless the paper also evaluates the method on real knowledge graph reasoning tasks. Also the transformer architecture is also quite similar to a recent graph transformer paper [5] that also introduces a node and edge token type embedding. Besides, the experiments seem significantly lacking, with details below.

(1) FB15k and WN18 are standard link prediction benchmarks, the datasets and settings really contradict with the motivation in the abstract “At a large scale, it becomes computationally expensive to aggregate useful information from the entire KG for inference”. First, I respectfully do not think FB15k and WN18 are large scale, there are larger benchmarks on the larger Freebase with tens of millions of nodes, I assume this is the right dataset for the authors to evaluate their model in order to support their claim; besides, if you want to make such a statement, you need to show how other methods are computationally expensive and how the proposed method is not, show the inference time. 

(2) Even on FB15k and WN18, the results are not complete, there are a full KG link prediction literature even within embedding-based methods going beyond RotatE, such as QuatE.

Some detailed (maybe repetitive) questions are listed below.
- The paper seems to ignore a large literature of knowledge graph question answering using retrieval based methods. [1,2] being two examples. These methods all propose retrieve-then-reason framework using GNNs. And the retrieval method is more expressive/adaptive than the ones proposed in this paper.
- Usually KG reasoning refers to a larger context of answering multi-hop complex queries [3,4]. Can the proposed method also do multi-hop reasoning?
- Can you also include the efficiency analysis of other methods in Table 2 as well?

[1] PullNet: Open Domain Question Answering with Iterative Retrieval on Knowledge Bases and Text
[2] Open Domain Question Answering Using Early Fusion of Knowledge Bases and Text
[3] Embedding Logical Queries on Knowledge Graphs
[4] Query2box: Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs in Vector Space Using Box Embeddings
[5] Pure Transformers are Powerful Graph Learners
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and easy to follow. The method is novel but the authors did not seem to have a thorough literature review of the baselines and the experiments do not support their motivation & statement. It seems reproducible with all the details listed in Sec. 4.3.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a retrieve-and-read framework for knowledge graph completion. The key motivation is that questions on knowledge graphs can usually be answered by a small subgraph. As such, they propose to first retrieve a subgraph from the complete knowledge graph with given entities and then perform reasoning over the small subset. To this end, they explored three retrieval strategies: BFS, One-hop neighborhood, and MINERVA, and a transformer is used in the read stage. They demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on two KG datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength 
- The proposed idea is straightforward.

### Weaknesses
- The task in the experiment is mainly about knowledge graph completion, which is only one-hop reasoning. While in the community, knowledge graph reasoning can be much more complex and may involve multi-hop reasoning and logical operations. Authors are referred to [a] for more details. If the authors claim contributions on knowledge graph reasoning, please follow this paper (and its follow-up work) and conduct more experiments.
- Within the scope of knowledge graph completion, the performance of the proposed model is weaker than the baselines. 
- The retrieve-and-read idea is not original; it has been widely explored in open-domain QA as described in Section 2. The model components are also not new; all of them are taken from existing work.


[a] Query2box: Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs in Vector Space using Box Embeddings, ICLR 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The model's novelty is limited, and the performance is also lower than many baselines. The claimed advantages of the proposed model cannot be verified and justified.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the novelty of this paper is limited. The experiment and the writing can be further improved. The claims cannot be supported by empirical results.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for link prediction in knowledge graph.  It employs a retrieve-and-read framework. In the first stage (retrieval), only a small relevant sub-graph from the KG is retrieved. In the second stage (reading), the retrieved sub-graph is fed into a high-capacity graph neural network for modeling. Experiments show that the proposed approach achieves good performance on two datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The overall retrieve-and-read framework is novel and interesting.

Weaknesses:
1. The retrieval stage is done with an off-the-shelf method (MINERVA). The reading stage is done by a deliberately designed graph neural network. For the reading stage modeling, I feel various existing graph neural networks can be applied. However, there lacks discussions and empirical comparison.
2. The performance of the proposed approach is not-so-good. The experiments are conducted in two datasets, only one of which demonstrates the superiority of the proposed approach. On the other dataset, the proposed model underperform the state-of-the-art method on two out of four metrics.
3. It seems the authors only evaluate entity prediction (given h and r, predict t), why not link prediction (given h and t, predict r)?

For weakness 1, just one example: Graph Transformer for Graph-to-Sequence Learning. I believe there are many similar papers.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- This paper is generally well-written. But I found Figure 2 confusing. What is the input question in this case?
- The general framework is novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall retrieve-and-read framework is novel and interesting. But the choices for both retrieval and reading stages seem ad-hoc. The empirical performance is not-so-good.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to address limitations of existing KG reasoning frameworks, including over-smoothing of representations and lack of scalability, and proposes a novel retrieve-and-read framework and develops a novel instantiation, KG-R3, for the framework, which retrieves a relevant subgraph context and reads with a Transformer-based GNN. 

#contributions
* This paper proposes a novel retrieve-and-read framework for knowledge graph reasoning with a novel instantiation, KG-R3, which retrieves a relevant subgraph context and reads with a Transformer-based GNN
* Empirical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the retrieve-and-read framework
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#Strength
* The paper proposes a novel retrieve-and-read framework for KG reasoning, which is intuitively effective

#Weaknesses
* The novelty is limited, as the framework is simple and lacks technical contributions
* Figure 3, illustrating the Reader module architecture, takes up much space while has little information contributions
* The motivation of the paper is to tackle limitations of existing KG reasoning frameworks, such as over-smoothing of representations and lack of scalability, but I didn’t find how the KG-R3 can make it. FB15K-237 & WN18RR are not large-scale KGs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity: Good. The paper is well organized but the presentation has minor details that could be improved
* Quality: Fair. The paper has minor technical flaws. For example, the proof of a theorem has some fixable errors or the experimental evaluation is weak.
* Novelty: Poor. The main ideas of the paper are not novel or have limited novelty.
* Reproducibility: The authors mentioned that all the code and data will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper has proposed a simple and effective framework for KG reasoning, which retrieves a relevant subgraph context and reads with a Transformer-based GNN. 
But the novelty is limited and experiments are not sufficient enough. The paper requires further improvement.
